#4807. How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It’s on every class schedule and all over your feed. So what does “sculpt” actually mean, and what can it do for you?

By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay. It’s an art form, a manipulation of material to achieve a desired end result that’s aesthetically appealing.

Over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture. We talk about sculpting one's back or legs, implying some kind of crafting of muscles, as if treating the human form like a sculpture. In fact, check the group class schedule of any gym these days, and you’ll likely spot the term “sculpt” appear somewhere on the lineup—directing toward some variation of a Pilates mat or strength training class, often involving lower weights and higher reps.

Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise? Is it a legitimate term or nothing more than strategic marketing language?

The exercise term actually dates back decades, with the first mentions appearing in fitness publications in the late 1970s. “It comes out of bodybuilding culture, which became more prominent in that period […] and you started to see the term ‘body sculpture,’” says Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, a historian and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. And while there’s no clear record of who coined the term in a fitness context, there is speculation that it may have been inspired by German strongman Eugen Sandow (often called the "father of modern bodybuilding"), who referenced Greco-Roman sculptures as examples of the “ideal” physique in the late 19th century.

In the 1980s, the idea of sculpting your muscles started to become much more mainstream, with the rise of aerobics, toning workouts, and fitness videos, says physical therapist and trainer Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, founder of Evlo Fitness. As instructors began using the term to describe and market workouts designed to shape and define specific muscles, “sculpting” became part of the everyday fitness vocabulary.

The term also taps into something more personal: this idea that we have the power to change the shape of our own physiques. “I think that it really gained momentum because one, it kind of speaks to the artistry of the body or the artistry of fitness. Also, there's so much individual agency in this,” says Petrezela. “It isn't about you just having the right genetics. Instead, you as an artist have the power to sculpt your own body.”

In the 1990s, however, the revered muscular look brought about by ’80s fitness culture made way for a celebration of thinner, more waifish bodies. “There was—and this is still the case—a lot of fear around getting too bulky,” says Petrezela. The term sculpting, however, molded into a promise of strength training without gaining too much muscle, which felt more palatable to women who feared such a physique.

“What's interesting is that we've changed the language over the years, but we're still selling women a very similar idea: that certain exercises will create a long, lean, toned appearance, while others will make them bulky,” says Ritchey.

If you worked out in the 2010s, you probably remember “sculpt” becoming a fixture of the boutique fitness boom. Still, while studio culture has waxed and waned over the last 20 years, the term has only gained traction, popping up across social media and on class schedules everywhere (think Pilates sculpt, yoga sculpt, and seemingly endless variations), notes Laura Girard, CPT, a NASM personal trainer and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Girard speculates that the popularity of sculpt classes may be buoyed by the widespread craving for more community in a post-pandemic world. After all, group fitness can be a fantastic third space. But there's another reason “sculpt” makes for such an appealing class name: It signals a particular kind of workout experience. Girard has observed “sculpt” used “almost like a dog whistle that [suggests] this class is going to be friendly for women and not scary, but still intense,” she says.

There's an aesthetic appeal, too. Petrezela believes the term’s resurgence of sorts has to do with how weightlifting and building muscle are very much having a moment, yet longstanding fears around getting “bulky” haven’t entirely disappeared. “It doesn't hurt that we are in a very, very image-driven moment in fitness culture,” she says. “We're not just looking at the images in magazines that come out once a month, but our [social media] feeds are nonstop bodies all day—many of which are shared by influencers who have their own plans for how you can sculpt a body that looks just like theirs, or so they say.”

If you were to ask 10 different people on the street what a “sculpt class” is, you may get 10 different answers. To some, sculpt is synonymous with a mat Pilates routine, to others it might be a strength-training session, and to others it might be a yoga practice involving light dumbbells. So, can all of these workouts really fall under the same umbrella? And when a class promises to “sculpt,” is that an actual measurable result your muscles can deliver—or a feeling the name is designed to sell?

According to the experts, it’s largely the latter. “In a world where two things are popular—strength training and being very thin—’sculpting’ seems to be an appealing middle ground from a marketing perspective,” says Ritchey. “It promises ‘long, lean muscle tone’ without the perceived risk of building too much muscle.”

She adds that “sculpt” is often used interchangeably with “toning,” which she describes as a “made-up term” that typically refers to changing your body composition (a.k.a., reducing fat and building muscle).

Because there's no single definition, what you actually do in a sculpt class can vary considerably. Still, Girard notes many sculpt classes share certain characteristics: lighter weights, choreography-inspired movements, and a lot of mat work. She also notes that while exercises are often fatiguing (think: that familiar muscle-burning sensation), they’re not necessarily pushing you to muscle failure via progressive overload (which is necessary for hypertrophy, or muscle-building).

Ritchey, who taught a sculpt class years ago, recalls using dumbbells and bodyweight for high reps. “We would do an entire three- to four-minute song of squats and lunges. That’s likely over 100 squats in a row, which burns and feels hard,” she says. Of course, it’s certainly possible to promote muscle-building with a low-weight, high-rep range, granted the programming is intentional. “But we know that if you could physically do more than about 30 reps in a row, the load is too light to build muscle.”

It’s important to note that a workout doesn't have to maximize muscle growth to be worthwhile. Certain sculpt classes can offer other benefits, from muscular endurance to simply providing motivation and enjoyment of exercising, often in a group setting. But if your primary goal is to significantly increase muscle size or change your body composition, not every sculpt class will provide the progressive resistance training needed to make that happen.

That’s where experts say the “sculpt” terminology can get confusing or misleading for some people. Girard fears that the language surrounding sculpt workouts reinforces misconceptions about women's bodies and what exercise can realistically change. “Sculpt as a verb is not a thing we can do to our bodies,” she notes. “We can gain or lose muscle. We can gain or lose fat, but that's more the role of nutrition. But we can't control how those muscles look.”

In other words, there's no special exercise technique that creates “long, lean” muscles instead of so-called “bulky” ones. Your genetics influence your muscle shape, while your training can affect how much muscle you build. And the workout's name doesn't change those underlying principles.

What’s more, at a time when there’s seemingly no consensus on how to talk about bodies or fitness in an empowering, nonoffensive way, Girard sees the term “sculpt” as potential coded language. While we may have mostly done away with, say, “bikini body shred” language in 2026, she fears that this nebulous term may be subliminally hinting at the same idea.

And while there's absolutely “nothing wrong with having aesthetic goals,” Ritchey stresses, “women deserve accurate information about how to achieve them.” If body recomp is their goal, they would have more success lifting close to failure and focusing on diet.”

Ultimately, your muscles don’t know whether you’re in a sculpt class or a traditional strength workout. Instead, they respond to the resistance, effort, and progression involved.

“It’s funny because while all these trends come and go—and we will see sculpt come and go, too—the science never changes,” Ritchey says. “People just aren’t patient enough with the basics, so they jump on the latest trend thinking it will finally be the golden ticket to seeing results.”

Because “sculpt” has no one definition, the quality, intensity, and overall experience of classes bearing the name can vary widely, too.

Beyond the workout itself, Girard points out that some sculpt classes can come with an unspoken expectation about who belongs in the room. As she’s observed: “These classes tend to be a self-selecting in-group. You may only see one type of body, or one specific outfit [...] That doesn’t mean it’s wrong or bad to be in a different outfit or in a different body, but it sure can feel that way.”

Of course, there are also plenty of classes with “sculpt” in the name that are fantastic, inclusive workouts. This all boils down to the instructor, methods, and specific exercises they choose to incorporate—along with the type of community they cultivate. And, in many cases—particularly with larger studios or gyms—instructors have no say in what their class is actually called. “A lot of times, they're just doing what's trending to get people in the door,” says Girard.

So if you’ve been curious to try a new sculpt class at a local studio—by all means, go for it. Just be sure to go into it with eyes wide open, and give yourself permission to stop or pause or walk away if it doesn’t feel like a productive or positive environment for you. Pay attention to how the workout feels, how the instructor coaches, and whether the environment makes you feel welcome. One potential red flag? Aggressive “bikini body” messaging or marketing that frames building muscle as something to avoid. As Girard emphasizes, “It is definitely, definitely is not.”

As the experts agree: Finding a form of movement you enjoy is the most important ingredient for establishing a healthy, consistent fitness routine. “My advice would be to ask yourself why you're doing these classes. Is it because you genuinely enjoy them? Or is it because you believe the burning sensation means you're toning and sculpting your muscles? Because those are two very different things,” says Ritchey.

Have a sculpt workout you absolutely love? That’s wonderful, too. Finding movement you genuinely enjoy is one of the best ways to build a fitness routine you'll actually stick with. The important thing is understanding what you're getting out of it—and whether that aligns with what you're hoping to achieve.

“I want women to feel empowered to choose exercise based on what they enjoy and what actually works,” says Ritchey.

For someone primarily focused on building muscle, Ritchey recommends treating sculpt classes as opportunities for cardio or simply enjoyable movement, rather than as a replacement for progressive strength training.

They can even be great options for off days from lifting. “I don’t want to discourage anyone from moving,” she says. “But at the same time, we deserve to understand what is marketing and what our bodies actually respond to. We are all busy and tired and stressed [and] I want women to know how to best use their efforts to match their goals.”

Appreciate the workout for what it is, understand what it isn't, and choose what works for you. That, in fact, is the true artistry of exercise.

Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, is a professor of history at the New School and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, is a physical therapist, fitness instructor, and founder of Evlo Fitness. Laura Girard, CPT, is a NASM-certified personal trainer, founder of The Energy Academy, and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

#4805. Jennifer Lawrence’s Hair Care Brand Launch Faced Public Scrutiny—But How Do the Products Actually Perform?

I tested Mes° Beauty for two weeks to find out.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

When Jennifer Lawrence joined Instagram in September, fans rejoiced at the idea of seeing more content from the actress known for her sarcastic humor and likable authenticity. In an already oversaturated beauty market, celebrity brands are a dime a dozen, and the announcement of Mes° Beauty didn’t exactly land well with the public. “She saw the numbers Rihanna, Selena Gomez, and Hailey Bieber were pulling in, and suddenly decided to join Instagram, too. Not necessarily to connect with her audience, but perhaps to tap into the same commercial machine and sell us even more stuff,” wrote one Instagram commenter.

JLaw teamed up with Jasmina Aganovic, founder of biotech beauty company Arcaea Labs, to formulate the brand’s hair care. As they say, the proof is in the pudding, so when I was sent all three products in a PR mailer, I knew I wanted to put them to the test.

Read my full, honest review of Mes° Beauty’s hair mask, serum, and volume mist below.

An intensive repair mask designed to be applied to dry hair anytime before washing. The milky-colored mask has a silky yet sticky, gelatin-like consistency that clings to your hair as you apply it. According to the brand, the mask prevents breakage and wash-day protein loss and protects the hair’s lipid barrier.

The Multitask Repair Mask differs from other hair masks because you apply it before shampooing and can leave it on for five minutes or overnight. With such a wide treatment time, it might take some trial and error to find the “sweet spot” for your hair type. During my testing, I applied a generous coat of the mask 5 to 10 minutes before shampooing. The second time, I tried applying a thinner coat of the mask, then pinned my hair up with a claw clip for about two hours before rinsing it out. The longer you wear it, the better the results. I would recommend applying a light coat before going about your day; that way, the scent isn’t overpowering and it won’t drip on your clothes.

After just two uses, my hair looked shinier and felt more hydrated after styling. As someone who rarely plans my hair care routine ahead of time, I appreciate that I can apply the mask just five minutes before I hop in the shower and still get noticeable results.

Although Mes° says the mask doubles as a styler for a glossy wet-hair look, I wouldn’t use it in that way. I think the product's consistency is too sticky and would be uncomfortable and messy (literally) to wear all day.

Some reviewers have mentioned a slightly off-putting smell. While the scent doesn’t bother me (it smells like a light, musky fragrance), it may not be for everyone. If I’m paying $52 for a hair mask, it would be nice to have a luxurious fragrance to add to the experience. If a brand is going to do musk, really lean into it with notes of sandalwood, amber, or patchouli.

The packaging also makes the product difficult to use. In the mailer I received, the mask comes in a GoGo Squeez-like pouch that you’re supposed to empty into the plastic tub. However, dipping my fingers into the tub felt clumsy, and next time I would just dispense directly from the pouch.

A bi-phase serum that smooths frizz, restores shine, and provides heat protection up to 450 degrees Fahrenheit. The “bi-phase” claim comes from combining a lightweight oil and a serum in the formula. After touching it, applying it, and letting it sit in my hair for a few days, I think calling it a serum is misleading. The consistency and the way it applies are much more like a hair oil.

On day two hair, I warmed two drops of the Off-Duty Restyling Serum between my palms, and worked it through my strands. I have very thick, straight, shoulder-length hair, so when I applied the serum up through my mid-lengths, it was way too oily. I don’t know if I would use it to restyle my hair unless I was planning to use a hot tool.

I also tested the serum as a finishing product, applying it to my ends after blow-drying. I found this to be the most effective way to use the product on my hair type.

Overall, the Off-Duty Restyling Serum doesn’t make much sense to me. What’s the point of having heat protection if it’s made for “reshaping yesterday’s style?” Are we going back in with more heat? To me, that sounds like an extra step in my morning routine that I do not have the time or patience for.

On days when I wash and blow-dry my hair, I like using a tiny amount of the serum just on my ends, and I've found it dries down nicely and leaves my hair soft and touchable. That said, I own other lightweight hair oils that work just as well for a fraction of the price—like FromLabs’ Protein Capsule Hair Repair Oil. If you have fine, wavy, or curly hair, the Off-Duty Serum may work better for you.

A lightweight spray that reduces scalp oiliness for lasting lift. Instead of creating gritty texture or absorbing excess oil like a dry shampoo, the Good Roots mist helps balance the scalp microbiome to produce less oil at the roots, extending the time until your next wash.

Over the past two weeks, I tested the Good Roots mist in three ways: applying it to damp hair before blow-drying, applying it to damp hair before air-drying, and applying it to dry day-two and day-three hair.

After about five uses of trial and error, I found it worked best when I applied it to my clean, damp roots and blow-dried. The heat felt like it helped dry down and “activate” the mist, whereas letting my hair air-dry didn’t produce much volume.

Pro-Tip: Be sure to hold the bottle about a foot away for even misting. The applicator pump doesn’t produce a fine spritz, and it took me a few uses to get that right.

After two weeks of testing, the Good Roots Volume Mist is my favorite of the trio. Two key ingredients, the proprietary Arc-5 Technology and the Mediterranean microalgae, help support a balanced scalp, keeping your hair fresher longer. With consistent use, the Good Roots mist extended my time between hair washes—I typically wash every other day, but I was able to go a third day. Plus, the Juniperus virginiana oil in the formula has a fresh, woody scent that reminds me of a fancy sea salt spray.

I also like that the mist doesn’t make my hair feel super gritty or textured the way a dry shampoo might. That said, I have other dry shampoo products that do a lot more heavy lifting than this volume mist. If I’m looking to achieve noticeable volume and lift in my thick hair, the Good Roots mist doesn’t cut it.

My general critique of Mes° Beauty is that the products are not very intuitive. They seem straightforward, but the brand doesn’t give great direction on how to get the most out of them. After the first one or two uses, you may feel they barely do anything at all. But if you learn how to use them properly when styling your hair, they can perform fairly well.

Mes° is supposed to be about “Less time fixing your hair. More time living,” but in reality, achieving that effortlessly chic, tousled look requires a fair bit of effort. In my opinion, this lineup is much more suited to someone who blows out or flat irons or curls their hair once or twice a week and wants to extend their style. For my hair type, these products don’t fit into my routine in a way that makes sense, but if you have fine and/or wavy hair, they might work better for you.

Curious about my other hair standbys? They’re currently $30 and under—and make for excellent beauty gift ideas for your loved ones for the upcoming holiday season.

#4803. Coldcard Bitcoin Exploit, Revisited: How a Hidden Flaw Survived Years of Audits

Coldcard Bitcoin Exploit, Revisited: How a Hidden Flaw Survived Years of Audits

Four months after attackers drained Bitcoin from compromised Coldcard hardware wallets, the device’s maker has published a detailed autopsy of how a single configuration error went undetected for more than five years, slipping past at least 15 separate security reviews before thieves exploited it.

The postmortem, released Monday by manufacturer Coinkite and modeled on an NTSB accident report, confirms the core failure when the exploit surfaced in July: from March 2021 through July 2026, Coldcard firmware generated wallet seeds using a software pseudo-random number generator, MicroPython’s Yasmarang, instead of the device’s intended hardware random-number generator.

The result was seeds with roughly 40 to 72 bits of effective randomness rather than the 128-bit target, weak enough for attackers to regenerate private keys offline and steal funds without ever touching a device.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The new report’s most revealing section is its accounting of why the flaw hid for so long.

Coinkite documented at least 15 independent review efforts between 2021 and 2026, including two paid third-party audits, physical-security work by Ledger Donjon, and even an AI-assisted firmware review that produced 85 findings. None caught it.

As the report puts it, every check “answered a nearby question rather than the critical one”: release checks confirmed the hardware-RNG code was present, but not that seed generation actually reached it, and statistical tests couldn’t distinguish the defective generator’s output from a properly seeded one.

A safeguard meant to reject the faulty configuration, a guard in the underlying libNgU code, simply didn’t work.

The scale of losses remains murky. Coinkite said it has received about 300 loss-related support tickets tied to 242 accounts, roughly 0.21% of its estimated user base, while Galaxy Research has attributed more than 8,600 addresses to the theft. The company cautions that those figures count different things and can’t be combined into a victim total.

One thread running through the report is the role of AI. Coinkite notes the first thefts began just two days after the Kimi K3 model’s full weights were released, calling AI-assisted discovery “a plausible hypothesis, not an attribution.”

It also documents how, after the flaw went public, the Bitcoin Red Team used Kimi K3 to run a 108-hour multi-model sweep that flagged nearly 8,000 candidate findings across 501 Bitcoin projects, underscoring how AI has upended the economics of vulnerability hunting.

Coinkite has since rebuilt its seed generation, adding mandatory user entropy, multiple hardware sources, and build-time and boot-time checks, with an independent review by Keylabs concluding the defect is “fully closed” in current standard firmware.

But no update repairs seeds already created on affected devices; those users must migrate to new ones. The report ends with a plea to whoever holds the stolen Bitcoin: return it.

“Some victims lost life-changing amounts, and returning the funds is the only action that can directly reduce that harm,” the company said.

#4802. Bitcoin sell-off driven by weak demand, forced liquidations: 21Shares

The crypto asset manager warned that Bitcoin’s downturn could persist amid weak investor demand, while forecasting an uneven recovery across crypto sectors.

The $6.4 billion hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance in October triggered Bitcoin’s recent sell-off, but weakening investor demand and forced liquidations drove most of the subsequent losses, according to a Nov. 24 report from crypto asset manager 21Shares.

While the Oct. 29 hack triggered the initial decline, the report found that weakening demand drove Bitcoin (BTC) down a further 8.3% between Nov. 4 and Nov. 11. Forced selling of leveraged positions led to the steepest decline, sending BTC down another 13.5% over the next three days. Crypto liquidations totaled $5.8 billion in the week ending Nov. 15, with long positions accounting for 81%.

Bitcoin’s sell-off and leverage unwind. Source: 21Shares

Signs of weakening demand were also seen in the stablecoin supply, which contracted by $10.7 billion following the hack, marking the largest 18-day decline in dollar terms since the Terra collapse in 2022. US spot Bitcoin and Ether (ETH) exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded combined outflows of $3.9 billion between Oct. 30 and Nov. 13.

Eliezer Ndinga, global head of research at 21Shares, told Cointelegraph that the market was already vulnerable before the hack:

The report also found little evidence of selling by other major Bitcoin holders. The 18,270 BTC and 522,409 ETH stolen in the Binance hack remained unspent as of mid-November, while neither the US government nor the Mt. Gox trustee had transferred Bitcoin to exchanges since the attack.

Bitcoin treasury firm Strategy continued buying, adding 2,332 BTC between Oct. 26 and Nov. 15. Meanwhile, miner transfers to exchanges fell to their lowest levels since at least 2020, although the data may not capture sales by publicly traded mining companies.

Related: Bitcoin slides amid US tariff nerves as Anthropic falls below IPO price

21Shares believes Bitcoin is already more than a year into a cyclical bear market. Historically, such downturns have lasted about two and a half years and resulted in average price declines of 84%, according to the report.

However, the researchers see a low probability of Bitcoin revisiting the depths of previous bear markets, citing the growing presence of institutional investors and spot ETFs. Ndinga said the competitive landscape for crypto has also changed:

Ndinga warned that a larger-than-expected Federal Reserve rate hike in December could prolong the downturn. Another potential source of selling pressure is the $2.2 billion in BTC and ETH stolen in the Binance hack, which could reach the market through over-the-counter (OTC) brokers in the coming months.

Ndinga identified Bitcoin’s realized price of $53,250, a measure of the average investor cost basis, as a key downside level to watch. Conversely, a return to the $73,000 to $75,500 range coupled with sustained ETF inflows and rising stablecoin balances would signal renewed investor demand.

#4801. 7 Running Shorts for Women That WH Editors Love

Editor-tested picks built for comfort, pockets, and sweat control.

There’s nothing more humiliating than having a huge sweat stain on your butt after strenuous mile repeats—been there, done that. A good run is supposed to lift your mood, not bring you down, so finding the best running shorts to keep the endorphins flowing (and your butt dry) is essential.

Not all workout shorts are made the same. Some offer more compression, while others are less restrictive and have convenient features like pockets—the holy grail! “You need a place to carry all your resources—pockets are a non-negotiable for running gels, electrolytes, phone, wallet, and keys,” says New York-based running coach and personal trainer Amanda Katz, NASM-CPT.

While many athletic shorts can be used for different purposes, running shorts usually have a built-in interior liner, sweat-wicking material, and a nonconstrictive design to keep you cool and comfortable as you rack up mileage in your sleek running shoes.

I researched and gathered the best running shorts from a running coach and editors who’ve personally tested them. Whether you’re training for a marathon or are a hobby jogger, all the shorts I picked are from trusted activewear and athleisure brands that will benefit you in the long run (literally). Ready to find out more about the best running shorts for women? Keep scrolling.

After testing countless pairs of running shorts over the years, the Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short from Lululemon is my fave for its sweat-wicking fabric and comfortable fit. The polyester blend wicks away sweat, prevents cling, and promotes airflow while running. The loose, flowy fit keeps me cool, while a built-in interior liner adds lightweight coverage and support without bulk.

The side pockets are small, but hold small essentials like a credit card, key, or energy gels for long runs. The leg openings are spacious, allowing for a full range of motion, and an adjustable drawstring secures the waistband for a customizable fit. Want to hit the road at the crack of dawn or at night? No sweat; reflective detailing improves visibility in dark or dim light, making early morning or evening runs safer.

I appreciate the 4-inch length, given I prefer more coverage, but a 2.5-inch length is available if you prefer a shorter fit. WH associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, is also a fan of the fit and vast color palette. “They never ride up or move around, which is hard to find in a running short,” she says. With tons of colors and sizes to choose from, you can't go wrong.

New Balance is a top brand in the running world, and the RC Short is one of my faves. It runs slightly big, but I love the extra breathing room during a sweat session.

The lightweight, flowy construction uses the brand’s quick-drying tech fabric (a polyester and spandex blend) to wick moisture from the skin. The breathable design promotes tons of airflow, creating a cooling effect while I run—especially ideal during scorching hot summer runs.

The seamless, interior lining reduces chafing and irritation, while the waistband features an adjustable drawstring to customize the fit. It’s also not too tight—some liners can feel like you’re wearing a diaper (hate). As for storage, there’s a back pocket for securing small running essentials and even tiny snacks like a granola bar when you’re on the move.

A pair of high cut shorts, such as the Alo Match Point Short, is a running staple. The high-cut at the thighs keeps things perfectly airy and flowy for optimal coolness when I get overheated, more so than the Lululemon Hotty Hot Short.

This construction, paired with its moisture-wicking polyester fabric, creates the perfect breathable running shorts. While it’s a bit short at just over two inches, there’s still great coverage with a built-in brief, and I find it doesn’t show too much skin.

WH style contributor Lily Wolhner also appreciates this loose style for various workouts. “My favorite part about this short is that it’s never clingy, so it doesn’t ride up the thigh or need constant re-adjusting while you’re working out,” Wolhner says. “I’ve worn it for months and recently tested it during a 45-minute strength and HIIT workout, as well as an hour-long cross-training workout—I never felt over-exposed or uncomfortable in it.”

By the looks of the elastic waistband, I expected it to dig into my skin—wrong. It felt comfortable, although it’s important to note this short does run big, so I suggest sizing down.

We love a two-for-one, and this short from Brooks is ideal for both trail running and running at the gym. It has light compression with a built-in tight liner that doesn’t sacrifice mobility.

The mega-durable polyester fabric resists tears and moisture, which makes it ideal for trail running in tough terrain. “I love the high waist, the zipper pocket to carry my keys, and the tight shorts under a looser short aesthetic,” Katz says.

Two waistband pockets are impressively large and can even fit a water flask, so you can always stay hydrated during your jogs.

I personally don’t love compression-lined shorts because I like to feel totally free, but if you prefer extra coverage and double layers, this short is ideal.

If you want a no-frills pair of shorts at an affordable price point that will stand the test of time, the Under Armour Play Up 3.0 belongs in your running gear collection. I’ve owned multiple pairs for years in eye-catching colors, and they’re still in good condition with no pills—even after dozens of runs and wash cycles.

The lightweight knit fabric made from smooth polyester has an anti-pill finish for extra durability, and is impressively comfy. Plus, it hides embarrassing sweat stains post-run, despite the slightly thicker material.

The waistband uses a wide elastic band that provides a secure fit without any adjustable features. However, I find it still fits roomy and allows for a full range of motion.

It includes deep side pockets but no enclosure, so I don’t recommend stashing anything super important besides fuel, like energy gels. I wear it the most for shorter, mid-distance runs and whenever I want to add a pop of color—it has 21 color options!

I usually don’t gravitate toward compression shorts since I don’t like feeling constricted, but the Athleta Salutation Stash 5-Inch Short offers the perfect amount of tightness. It hugs my thighs with gentle compression, while the high-rise waistband distributes pressure evenly for a secure fit without digging in. Plus, the two deep side pockets offer convenient storage for longer runs.

The smooth, double-knit fabric is buttery-soft and offers great coverage. While on the thicker side, it conceals sweat stains well—a huge win during long-haul runs. I wouldn’t say it feels the most breathable compared to other shorts in this guide, but the nylon and lycra blend wicks away sweat and dries fast.

Another huge selling point? The fabric’s UPF 50 protection, which prevents UV radiation from scorching your thighs. This is my favorite feature as someone fair-skinned and prone to nasty sunburns (IYKYK). Aside from its fabric, I love that it has a matching jacket for a coordinated workout set.

Tracksmith’s Van Cortlandt Shorts combine retro styling with a performance-driven design that makes them a winner both on and off the track. It’s made from a lightweight mesh fabric to maximize airflow, paired with an antimicrobial finish to help combat odor by wicking away sweat and limiting bacteria buildup during intense runs.

After summer runs when I’m dripping with sweat, I noticed zero smell—and that the short dries at the speed of light.

Like our best overall, it’s quite short at 2.5 inches, so if you prefer a longer style, you should look to other styles in this guide. On the flip side, it doesn’t disrupt my range of motion during speed work or long runs. As for fit, I found it runs true to size, but make sure to consult the size chart as always.

Running shorts with sweat-wicking fabric are the way to go, Katz says. Most shorts use a blend of polyester, spandex, and/or nylon, which lifts moisture from the skin while staying flexible during movement. Based on testing, it’s best to avoid cotton since it doesn’t dry nearly as fast and clings to the skin when wet.

It’s important to determine what kind of rise and inseam you desire. High-waisted running shorts offer more coverage and tummy control, while a mid-rise waist sits right at the hips. Ultimately, what you find most flattering for your body type is the best option.

The inseam is the length from the crotch to the bottom. A longer length will show less skin but may disrupt the range of motion, while some running shorts favorites, like the Lululemon Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short, offer a 2.5-inch option if you like a mini fit.

As for an interior liner or compression, this will make running shorts fit more snugly. “Compression is a matter of preference, but the goal in this material is to boost recovery,” says Katz. If you want a less constrictive fit, it’s probably best to avoid that feature.

In addition to my own testing, Women’s Health associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT also extensively tested tons of running shorts to determine whether or not they’re the real deal. Each pair was worn during training runs or races for anywhere from three weeks to even three years to see how they performed and held up.

Essential features considered were materials, inseam, pockets, durability, and adjustability. Additionally, I asked a running coach for their go-to running shorts and guidance on how they should fit.

#4799. Anthropic’s Claude Ship Lets AI Write, Review and Approve Its Own Code

Anthropic’s Claude Ship Lets AI Write, Review and Approve Its Own Code

Anthropic is automating another part of software engineering: the process of deciding whether the code an AI writes is actually good enough to use.

The company introduced Claude Ship on Monday, a collection of AI agents capable of reviewing software changes, fixing errors, and approving code according to rules established by development teams.

Under certain configurations, software changes can make their way into a company's codebase without a human reading a single line of code.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

AI coding tools have become so good at producing software that reviewing it has become a bottleneck. Developers who previously spent hours writing a feature can now generate several in that time, but someone still has to check whether those changes work without breaking something else.

Anthropic is experiencing that problem itself. The company says Claude already writes most of the code produced by its Claude Code team.

Claude Ship combines three tools, each responsible for a different stage of the process. The first, Code Review, examines proposed changes against the existing codebase, using multiple agents to find potential bugs and verify each other's findings.

PR Steward, the second tool, makes the necessary corrections when automated tests fail or reviewers identify problems. It documents its modifications and provides instructions for reversing them, allowing developers to intervene if necessary.

The third tool, Claude Approvals, decides whether the proposed changes satisfy the company's approval policies. According to Anthropic's technical documentation, repositories configured for automatic merging can incorporate changes without anyone manually approving them.

The ability to delegate code reviews to AI is particularly attractive in the age of vibe coding, where developers—and increasingly people with little programming experience—build software by describing what they want in natural language.

But having an AI double-check another AI's work doesn't necessarily eliminate their shared weaknesses. A human programmer and a language model might approach a problem differently, whereas two agents powered by similar models could overlook the same flawed assumption.

A peer-reviewed study published earlier this year found that models from OpenAI and Anthropic performed slightly better at identifying and repairing security vulnerabilities in human-written code than in AI-generated code.

AI-assisted software development has already produced some expensive mistakes. In April, a startup founder reported that a coding agent running Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 deleted his company's production database and its volume-level backups through a single API call.

Anthropic's own experience with automated code reviews illustrates a different problem: AI agents can get stuck correcting each other. In one instance, according to an October engineering report, a proposed software change went through more than 50 rounds of automated reviews and corrections overnight before its author intervened.

The company nevertheless reported encouraging internal results. The number of merged changes more than doubled between June and September, while the proportion of changes that had to be reversed fell by more than 40%.

Those results came from a broader review process that retained human oversight for sensitive modifications, rather than a fully autonomous system. Changes to documentation can pass without human approval at Anthropic, whereas particularly risky modifications require two people to sign off.

“A person is accountable for every change that ships, whoever typed it,” Anthropic's engineers wrote.

Whether other companies adopt equally restrictive policies is up to them. Claude Ship allows administrators to determine which parts of their software require human supervision and which decisions they are comfortable delegating to an AI.

The service is available for GitHub repositories on Claude Team and Enterprise plans, with charges based on token consumption. For now, Anthropic recommends running its automated approval system in observation mode, letting the AI demonstrate what it would have approved before giving it the authority to do so.

#4798. Utah moves to dismiss criminal charges against Kalshi after trading halt

Utah’s attorney general warned that the criminal charges could be refiled if Kalshi resumes operations in the state, while separate civil litigation remains unresolved.

Utah’s attorney general has moved to dismiss 14 criminal charges against prediction market platform Kalshi and its two co-founders after the company blocked users in the state from accessing its services.

The attorney general’s office said it filed a motion Monday to dismiss the case without prejudice in Utah’s Third District Court, allowing prosecutors to refile the charges if Kalshi resumes operations in the state.

The office opened a criminal investigation into Kalshi in September and filed charges on Oct. 28, alleging that the company offered illegal gambling to Utah residents. Kalshi subsequently agreed to block access to its platform in the state and monitor attempts to reach its services from Utah-based IP addresses.

“Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Attorney General Derek Brown said, adding that his office would continue to enforce state gambling laws against other prediction market operators.

The office also sent cease-and-desist letters to several of Kalshi’s competitors, with six other prediction market companies agreeing to stop operating in Utah.

Kalshi General Counsel Yaakov Roth said in a Tuesday post on X that “good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized,” adding that the company was willing to work with state attorneys general while courts resolve the regulatory dispute.

The case is separate from a civil lawsuit Utah brought against Kalshi and its market-making partner Susquehanna International Group on Oct. 20, seeking restitution, damages and the recovery of proceeds from allegedly illegal gambling activities. The complaint estimates that Kalshi collected between $30.6 million and $61.2 million in fees from Utah-based accounts as of Oct. 19.

The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) announced its own lawsuit against Utah on Oct. 27, seeking to block the state from enforcing its gambling laws against federally regulated prediction markets. The lawsuit is part of a broader legal battle over the regulation of prediction markets, with the CFTC asserting exclusive jurisdiction over event contracts. The federal regulator has sued at least 12 states over the issue.

Many of the leaves in Central Park are turning a gorgeous burnt-orange hue, and hot apple cider is readily available at local cafes and farmers' markets. But like clockwork every fall since moving to New York from Florida, my skin has been feeling dry, tight, and a little itchy. My complexion is also a little flushed after cleansing, which isn’t the norm during the spring and summer.

Turns out that I’m not alone. Dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD, says her patients often experience rough or flaky patches, dullness, and increased sensitivity to products they previously tolerated well after cleansing this time of year. They also notice tightness, itching, and products that suddenly sting. Sure, cranking up my pretty pink Canopy humidifier can help a little, but after talking with dermatologists, it’s officially time to upgrade my skincare routine for fall.

The good news: We don’t need to replace our entire routine this fall. Dermatologists share their ideal morning and night skincare tweaks. Plus, they reveal how to safely exfoliate dry, flaky skin, and weigh in on using retinoids. The best part? Many of their suggestions are drugstore staples from brands like Cetaphil and La Roche-Posay.

“A healthy barrier does not require a ten-product supporting cast,” says Dr. Gohara. You really only need a few key items—and you may even have them in your home already. Here’s a roundup of dermatologist-recommended products the pros agree are worthy of a spot in your skincare routine. I also included my favorite face sunscreen for the morning and eye cream for twice daily use.

Dr. Nazarian swears by this Cetaphil option and calls it her top cleanser because it's, well, super gentle. She highlights the trifecta of glycerin, niacinamide, and panthenol, as a major win for your skincare game. Notably, glycerin is a humectant to hold onto moisture.

Aveeno Positively Radiant Vitamin C Serum

“Glow with a built-in comfort crew,” says Dr. Gohara about this Skincare Award-winning face serum. “Vitamin C is a proven skin-brightening, collagen-boosting powerhouse. The only problem: it’s known to be irritating on sensitive skin. Aveeno has solved for that here, adding a calming concoction of niacinamide and the brand’s famed oat complex,” says beauty director Brian Underwood.

We’ve previously named this the best overall hyaluronic acid serum and Dr. Nazarian agrees. She appreciates that it boasts multiple forms of hyaluronic acid to enhance hydration, adding that it’s a great serum for layering with other products in your routine.

You can slather this budget-friendly moisturizer on your face and body. It earned snaps from Dr. Gohara, who points to the combination of glycerin to attract water and ceramides to support the skin barrier.

Pro tip from Dr. Gohara: Whether you use a lotion or a face cream, apply it to slightly damp skin.

For extra dryness, layer SkinMedica Barrier Calming Cream on top, advises Dr. Gohara. “Just as you double up on clothes, you can double up on moisturizer. Hydration first, a protective outer layer second,” she says. And that’s exactly what the Barrier Calming Cream does. It contains a nourishing blend of moisturizing glycerin, niacinamide to minimize skin inflammation, and calming oat kernel extract.

The experts I chatted with say eye cream is a totally optional step. You can technically get away with just using a plain face moisturizer under your eyes, says Dr. Nazarian. However, since the undereye skin is thinner and prone to dryness during colder months, a separate eye cream can be helpful for dealing with dryness, fine lines, or crepiness.

Neocutis combines human growth factors with a proprietary blend of peptides to target fine lines, wrinkles, puffiness, and dark circles. After about two weeks, I noticed my undereye area was a little more luminous.

Isdin Eryfotona Actinica Mineral Sunscreen SPF 50+

You shouldn’t retire your sunscreen in the fall, argues Dr. Gohara. A broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher sunscreen is a daily staple. My all-time favorite one is the Isdin Eryfotona Ageless—it’s a tinted mineral sunscreen that doesn’t leave a ghastly finish on my face. It contains plankton-derived DNA Repairsomes, which Isdin says help repair existing sun damage. The formulation is lightweight and absorbs quickly and it’s even water-resistant for active lifestyles.

SkinMedica HA5 Hydra Collagen Facial Mist

Spritz your skin with this spray whenever your complexion needs extra TLC. Dr. Gohara calls this your skin’s “hydration intermission.” It moisturizes and helps keep water in, and layers beautifully over makeup.

Before you go to bed and watch TV, you’ll want to do your skincare routine. You can use pretty much everything from your morning routine.

This creamy cleanser is great for seasonal dryness.

Pro tip from Dr. Garshick: Avoid washing with very hot water since it can contribute to dryness. If you have very sensitive skin, consider splashing your face with water instead of cleansing twice daily, she says.

"This eye cream is rich without being heavy so it won’t leave skin with an oily finish,” says dermatologist Joshua Zeichner, MD, in our 2020 Skincare Awards. He loves that it can “help strengthen the skin and improve texture and fine lines—no irritation in sight."

Lock in hydration with this lightweight face serum that doesn’t feel overly tacky on your skin.

SkinMedica makes a slew of impressive products, including a recent 2026 Skincare Award win for the Exfoliating Pads. However, when you’re shopping for a moisturizer for fall, consider this investment-worthy pick. While pricey, you only need a few small dabs of cream all over your face.

Dr. Nazarian suggests Dermal Repair Cream to anyone who wants to use a retinoid product in the fall. “It’s incredibly hydrating and calming—and uses a form of hyaluronic acid combined with vitamins C and E for skin hydration and environmental defense along with a gentle form of retinoid,” she says. Just be sure to gradually introduce it into your routine.

In the fall, it’s all about hydration. Both Dr. Garshick and Dr. Nazarian suggest humectants such as glycerin and hyaluronic acid to attract water, plus skin barrier-supporting ingredients such as ceramides. You might also benefit from slathering on a richer cream packed with fatty acids, shea butter, or squalane if your skin is very dry.

Yes, you can exfoliate in the fall, but only occasionally. TBH, the frequency varies based on your specific needs and the product you’re using. But you can probably start with once a week or even every two weeks if you have more sensitive skin. You should also avoid scrubbing irritated skin and not exfoliate the same night you use a retinoid while building tolerance. “Flakes are not an invitation to scrub harder,” says Dr. Gohara. “You are polishing skin, not refinishing furniture.” Also, don't be afraid to pause exfoliating if your skin ever feels uncomfy. You can just use your classic face moisturizer until your skin feels comfortable again, adds Dr. Gohara.

Look, just because it’s overcast and chilly out doesn’t mean you should skip wearing sunscreen in the fall. And don’t just take my word for it: “Your sweaters have seasonal employment; your sunscreen works year-round,” says Dr. Gohara. That means you should wear a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher on your exposed skin, including your ears, neck, and hands. Follow your sunscreen label for specific reapplication tips, but typically, you can reapply at least every two hours and after sweating or swimming, according to the American Academy of Dermatology.

The experts I spoke with say you can use a retinoid year-round if your skin can tolerate it and if you diligently reapply sunscreen. However, fall is a convenient time to add a retinoid—such as retinol, retinal, tretinoin, or adapalene—into your routine. Regardless of which type of retinoid you select, start using it gradually. Dr. Garshick says two or three times a week is a good jumping off point, then you can increase frequency as tolerated.

#4790. The 8 Best Standing Desks for Walking Pads, Tested and Reviewed

From budget picks to tricked-out options for a better WFH space.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

You log a lot of time at your desk, making it fair to wonder how to create a workspace that’s as comfortable and healthy for you as possible. If sitting on your butt all day isn’t your idea of a good time, it makes sense to consider investing in a walking pad. To create a seamless workspace, you’ll need a special desk to go with that. The best standing desks for walking pads allow you to cruise along as you work, while still providing all the usual trappings you expect from a desk.

While TikTok is packed with happy-looking people working this way, the treadmill desk is more than a trend. Research ties sitting all day with a higher risk of developing back pain and even issues with cardiovascular health, making it a good idea to try to get up and move as much as possible during your day.

“Prolonged sitting has been linked to a number of health concerns, which is why many people are turning to standing desks,” says Andrew J. Bach, DO, a physiatrist at Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles “A standing desk allows you to get your usual computer-based work done while on your feet, and it comes with several benefits over sitting all day.” (He lists off better circulation, less strain on your back, more calories burned, and better digestion as just a few.)

But proper form is critical with these. “People should keep in mind how long they have been in a certain position, and their posture specifically,” says Meg Darmofal, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University. You don’t want to shrug your shoulders, reach too far forward, bend over, or crane your neck up or down to see your screen, she says—all of those can put you at risk for developing aches and pains.

To find the best standing desks for walking pads, we consulted experts and had Women's Health editors test several popular models in their own workspaces. Our top pick is the Uplift Standing Desk V3, thanks to its easy height adjustments, customizable design, and compatibility with a walking pad. Ahead, find our favorite options for different budgets, spaces, and work-from-home setups.

While everyone has different needs in a standing desk, the Uplift V3 is packed with enough features and adjustability to make it a good fit for most. This motorized desk has a height range of 22.6 to 48.7 inches and comes in a wide range of tabletop widths and desktop styles, giving you plenty to choose from.

The desk has an impressive 355-pound lifting capacity, so you can pile a lot on it. WH copyeditor Deanna Martin tested the V3 alongside a walking pad and loved how easily the setup transformed her home office. The desk moves up and down with the touch of a keypad, making it easy to switch between sitting, standing, and walking throughout the workday.

Martin also liked the customizable accessories, which include storage options and even a hammock. There's also a companion app that tracks your standing progress and estimated calorie burn, though you'll need a Bluetooth adapter to connect it to the desk. Best of all, she found the entire setup super easy to assemble.

At over $600, the V3 is certainly an investment. But its versatile design, smooth height adjustments, and 15-year warranty are worth the price point.

It’s fair to expect to pay more for a motorized standing desk, but this Flexispot option manages to deliver that important feature with a relatively low price tag. The desk moves between 28 and 47.6 inches, giving you plenty to work with. It also has four height presets operated by an LED control panel, and a relatively roomy desktop space.

The desk includes a hook for your headphones or bag, allowing you to keep them in close reach while you work. It also can handle 176 pounds of weight, which should be plenty to work with. While it doesn’t have as many features as pricier desks like the Uplift 3, it’s still a solid, sturdy option to support you through your workday and comes much more affordably.

Whether you already have a desk you like or just don’t want to splash out for a totally new model, a standing desk converter can be a good middle ground. This option from Rocelco simply plops on top of your existing table to create a standing desk, so you can use a walking pad without replacing your entire WFH setup.

While some standing desk converters are small, this one can hold up to two large monitors, a laptop, and more. There’s a retractable keyboard tray, although it may not extend far enough for everyone's needs. The height adjustment is manual, but easy to do with the turn of a dial. There’s even a grommet hole to help you organize your cords, giving you a lot of the perks of a standing desk without the full commitment. Just make sure your existing desk and converter are tall enough to accommodate your walking pad.

A contoured standing desk allows you to get in close to your workspace, with an ergonomic design that can help you maintain a comfortable position while walking on a treadmill. This Fully Jarvis desk is sleek and comfortable, with a gently sloping and curved front that feels natural under your arms.

During testing, we were able to put this desk together quickly. It has a very sturdy feel, which is helpful when you’re walking while using it. The desk also thoughtfully includes an outlet and USB/lightning charger, so you can plug in your computer without having to bend over. The motor adjusts easily, although it can be a little choppy when you move up and down. Overall, we found that it was easy and comfortable to use. It looks and feels like a high-quality desk thanks to its bamboo surface and sturdy steel frame, making this a workspace you’ll use for years.

Having a little extra storage space can go a long way when you're trying to keep your home office organized. This Sanodesk standing desk features built-in drawers to stash away your office clutter. It's also motorized, so you can easily adjust the height when you want to sit, stand, or hop on your walking pad.

WH Designer Taryn Colbert tested the desk for two weeks and gave it a four out of five. She liked its spacious, easy-to-clean surface and preset heights. “It’s perfect,” she says, adding that it was “easy to put together for a person thats not very handy.”

Her biggest gripes? She wished the power plug were positioned farther toward the back of the desk, rather than toward the front and side, and would have preferred a long, slim drawer for additional storage.

This electric standing desk from Veken has a compact design that won't take over your home office, along with a motorized height adjustment system that makes it easy to switch between sitting and standing. There are also programmable height presets, so you don't have to find your preferred position every time.

WH Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey tested the desk for two to four weeks and gave it a five out of five. She was super impressed by how sturdy it felt, even when raised to its maximum height. “It feels well made for a desk that the buyer assembles (no shaky IKEA feeling here, even when at its max height!),” she says. Ritchey also liked the easy-to-use height adjustments and wide range of positions.

Her biggest gripe was the size. While the 36-inch desktop was great for occasional use, she wished she'd gone up a size for everyday work. She also found the textured surface a little tricky to clean after spills.

This walking pad features a removable desktop that attaches to the treadmill's railings, giving you a convenient spot for your laptop or tablet while you clock your steps. WH Lifestyle Director Lindsay Geller tested the setup for over a month and gave it a five out of five. She especially liked how sturdy the desktop felt once attached and how easy it was to remove. “This is a really great way to get a second desk without actually committing to buying a full desk,” she says, noting that she shares a home office with her husband. She also found assembly straightforward, putting the entire setup together by herself in about an hour.

The desk is admittedly basic, and the treadmill doesn't offer adjustable incline. Geller also found the walking surface a little narrow for jogging, making this a better option for walking while working than more intense workouts.

Every standing desk has either a set height or height range. Bach points out that height is a “key factor” in your desk. “If you’re especially tall or short, make sure the desk can adjust to a level that works for you,” he says. Just keep in mind that you’ll want to include the height of your walking pad when figuring out the right standing desk height for you, since you’ll be on top of it while you use your desk. “Returning a bulky standing desk can be a hassle, so it’s best to get the right fit from the start,” Bach says. Ideally, your desk should be high enough that you can type comfortably while standing on your walking pad, without having to hunch over or raise your shoulders.

Not all standing desks are adjustable, but many are—and it’s a nice feature to have. “Being able to easily lower and raise the desk is important because, in some scenarios, returning to sitting is good as well,” Darmofal says. Some desks can be heavy and awkward to move manually, which can be frustrating if you plan to switch between sitting and standing during the day, Bach says. “Motorized options are the most convenient, since they transition with the push of a button,” he adds. (Just keep in mind that motorized options tend to cost more.)

At the end of the day, this is still a desk, and you need one that will hold your stuff. Make sure you factor in space to hold your computer, pens, notepad, water bottle, and anything else you usually have on your desk. If you're using a walking pad, you'll also want enough room for your keyboard and monitor so you don't have to lean forward while walking.

It’s important to make sure that your desk’s legs and any footing are wide enough to leave space for your walking pad to slip between. Pay close attention to the walking pad dimensions and desk dimensions, leaving a little room around the pad so you’re not jamming it in there.

We should also note that a lot of our standing desk selections below don't come with a walking pad (though the Sharper Image Treadmill Desk is an all-in-one option), meaning it's an additional expense. If you don't already have one, make sure to check out our under-desk treadmill buying guide.

I consulted with Bach and Darmofal to help identify what to look for in standing desks for walking pads. From there, I researched top models, narrowing the field based on criteria like comfort, adjustability, and ease of use. Because everyone has a different experience, I also paid close attention to customer reviews and prioritized desks with overwhelmingly positive feedback.

From there, Women's Health editors put several standing desks to the test in their own workspaces. Our testers included Cori Ritchey, Lindsay Geller, Taryn Colbert, and Deanna Martin, who evaluated the desks for build quality, ease of assembly, adjustability, size, and overall functionality. Testing periods ranged from one week to over a month, with editors using their desks while sitting, standing, or walking on an under-desk treadmill. We also considered how stable each setup felt, how easily it fit into a home office, and any drawbacks our testers encountered.

#4788. Europol follows $28.5M crypto trail in streaming piracy crackdown

Authorities from 11 countries worked with Binance, Coinbase and Chainalysis to trace financial transactions and disrupt illegal streaming services.

Law enforcement authorities from 11 countries, working with crypto exchanges Binance and Coinbase and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, have traced more than 26 million euros ($28.5 million) in cryptocurrency transactions and disrupted 57 illegal streaming services in an operation coordinated by Europol, the law enforcement agency of the European Union.

In a Tuesday announcement, Europol said the five-day operation took place in Seville, Spain, from Nov. 16 to Nov. 20 and identified 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content, attracting more than 7.3 million annual visits combined.

Europol said illegal streaming operators often collect subscription payments in cryptocurrency, allowing them to transfer funds quickly across borders. Investigators traced blockchain transactions to identify links between streaming services, cryptocurrency wallets and the individuals controlling them.

The EU’s law enforcement agency said the operation reflects a shift from focusing solely on shutting down illegal streaming services to also targeting the financial infrastructure behind them. The findings will support ongoing national investigations, including efforts to identify suspects and trace assets linked to criminal activity.

According to figures from the Audiovisual Anti-Piracy Alliance cited by Europol, an estimated 60 million people across Europe use unauthorized internet protocol television (IPTV) services, with estimated annual losses of 4.83 billion euros ($5.3 billion) for legitimate providers and a further 1.08 billion euros ($1.18 billion) in unpaid taxes for governments.

Related: Tron and Tether bring in Chainalysis after T3 crime unit folds

The operation follows other international efforts to disrupt criminal networks and their financial infrastructure. In March, US and European authorities dismantled SocksEscort, a malicious proxy service that enabled crimes including bank fraud and cryptocurrency account takeovers.

The service allowed customers to pay anonymously in cryptocurrency and received at least $5.7 million in user payments, according to investigators. Authorities froze about $3.5 million in cryptocurrency linked to the operation.

Earlier that month, Europol and the FBI took down LeakBase, a cybercrime forum with more than 142,000 registered users. An earlier cybercrime marketplace, RaidForums, had previously hosted leaked personal data belonging to users of crypto hardware wallet provider Ledger.

#4787. Raving in Your 40s, 50s, and 60s? These Women Say It’s the Best Self-Care They’ve Found

Why women are turning to the EDM scene in the name of mental health.

Ask Karen Manson, 65, how she likes to recharge, and she’ll tell you this: a night of pounding bass, a sweaty dance floor, and getting home in the wee hours of the morning. She’s loved music her whole life and was always drawn to EDM, but marrying and having kids young left little room to explore it. Then, three years ago, her husband died, and she began thinking about how short and precious life is—and decided it was time to push herself to try new experiences.

That’s how she ended up at her first rave last year, solo. She was nervous, but spent the night dancing, and left with new friends and a newfound confidence. “I felt uninhibited,” she says. She’s attended more than 20 raves since.

Manson isn’t an outlier. Midlife women are prioritizing their mental health now more than ever, according to a 2026 study in the journal Women’s Health that analyzed nearly 1,000 surveys about women’s health priorities and concerns. And a number of them are finding relief on the dance floor.

A 2025 study in Psychology of Music surveyed 136 women ages 40 to 65 about why they’re involved in EDM experiences. The overwhelming response was that raving was a meaningful part of their mental well-being—an outlet for stress, a source of connection, and a rare place to escape the demands of everyday life, according to the survey.

“There is a rise in older people attending electronic dance music events, raves, clubs, parties, festivals,” says Alice O’Grady, PhD, a professor of applied performance at the University of Leeds, who co-authored the Psychology of Music study. “The motivations for women going are pretty much characterized as the same as they are for any age: the love of the music, the ability to socialize with existing friends, the atmosphere of the environment, and the sense of community.” Put simply: These music events are plain fun.

The EDM scene is no longer the epitome of youth culture, O’Grady adds, and it’s become more socially acceptable for women to embrace this genre of joy as they get older. That shift may reflect changing attitudes about aging, with women potentially feeling less constrained by traditional expectations about how they’re “supposed” to spend their time as they age. Social media has also made it much easier to discover niche music scenes, while a growing focus on mental health, movement, pleasure, and community may be encouraging women to seek out experiences that just make them feel good.

The older you get, the harder it can be to find a place where you can be playful, spontaneous, and fully present with other people. For some, the rave scene provides exactly that. “You've got more responsibility, more commitments,” O’Grady says. “You want that escape, you want that ability to connect through music and immerse yourself in an environment that allows you to be expressive and just shake off some of those roles that older women carry.”

Samantha Hillery, 43, started raving in her 20s as a way to let loose and have fun. But as life got busier with work, family, and kids, she stopped going. Years later, while searching for fun things to do in her area with friends, she came across Bingo Loco, a high-energy party with EDM, dancing, confetti, and—yes—bingo, and found her way back to it.

Now, Hillery gives herself permission to step away from the endless list of adult responsibilities. “As we get older and super busy with our lives, we forget how fun we maybe used to be, and it seems like something that was so far in the past,” she says. “But when you’re able to go out and rave surrounded by a bunch of friends and people that just want to have a good time, you remember that part of you isn’t lost.”

For some, keeping up with friends also becomes more challenging as you age and enter new eras of your life. Social obligations often come second, competing with work schedules, children, relationships, and other obligations, says Madison Liddle, LMHC, a licensed psychotherapist and founder of Pattern Psychology. At a music event like these, though, spontaneous connection is built into the experience.

Hundreds or thousands are gathered around the same music, moving to the same rhythm, creating an immediate sense of belonging. It’s a concept called collective effervescence, which is “a feeling of joy and connection when a group of people are in a shared space doing a shared thing,” Liddle explains. “Social connection is a really strong determinant of health as we age, and raving offers an opportunity to create and be in community with people with shared interests.”

Getting out and meeting new people is the main reason Manson is so attracted to rave culture—she’s found the crowds to be welcoming and friendly. “Life can become quite small if you don't push yourself,” she says, alluding to feeling alone after her husband’s passing. “I enjoy meeting people, I enjoy conversations. I'm not good at home in my own company—I need socialization.” Dancing with new friends is the way to do that, and it keeps her feeling energized.

In fact, in Manson’s experience, the EDM scene has seemed remarkably friendly to people of all ages and backgrounds. O’Grady agrees: “Women need spaces that are inclusive, welcoming, and accessible, and the rave scene actually does that quite well,” says O’Grady. You’ll feel a sense of belonging, like you’re part of something bigger than yourself, even if you’re there alone, she adds. The music creates an instant common language, while dancing alongside friends and strangers turns what could be an individual activity into something meaningful and collective.

The physical perks of dancing are well documented. It strengthens the cardiovascular, metabolic, musculoskeletal, and cognitive systems, as WH previously reported. It can also improve coordination, balance, and stability, which becomes especially important with age. But it can boost your mental health too, mainly because it helps you stay present. When you’re fully focused on what you’re hearing, feeling, and doing, there’s less room to get caught up in the mental replaying and worrying that can fuel stress, Liddle says.

In fact, many participants in the Psychology of Music study described dancing at raves as a way to ease anxiety, depression, and low moods, says co-author Alinka Greasley, PhD, a professor of music psychology at the University of Leeds. Anxiety can keep the mind focused on what might go wrong, while depression can make the present feel flat.

Raving, by contrast, demands attention in a different way. Instead of sitting with your thoughts, you’re listening to loud, immersive music, dancing to the beat, and anticipating the next drop, Liddle explains. That physical engagement helps interrupt rumination and creates a sense of clarity that lasts beyond the dance floor; it can help clear your head.

Alex Daly attended her first EDM show at 40 after her partner, who’d been going to raves for years, encouraged her to come along. A year later, raving has become a central part of her wellness routine. If she’s having a stressful week and doesn’t have an EDM show on her calendar, she immediately starts looking for one. “Once I’m in the crowd, I get into a flow state, and moving my body to the beat really helps me process my emotions,” says Daly, now 41. “Dancing helps me stop ruminating, get out of my head, and back into my body.” For a few hours, there’s simply less room for the mental noise of everyday life. In a way, it’s like the pounding beat is a reset button you can dance to.

Of course, rave culture has long been tied to recreational drugs like MDMA, which can bring on feelings of euphoria, connection, and stress relief. That link hasn’t disappeared. Some of the women in the Psychology of Music study said they took drugs, often to keep their energy up for dancing, while others went purely for the music and the movement.

However, drugs weren’t what gave the women a sense of belonging, the study uncovered. “That's very much already there from their perspective,” Greasley says. “The drugs are more to do with [increasing] energy levels and also the marrying of the drugs and the music. Many women called it a spiritual experience to be in ecstatic states whilst dancing to the music.”

Karen D., 62, who asked that her last name be withheld because she discusses her drug use, sees it the same way. She started going to raves in her early 50s with her second husband. While she partakes in recreational drug use, she also knows people who attend raves completely sober. For her, the bonding comes from dancing with like-minded people who are all just happy to be there.

But Karen acknowledges that drugs heighten those feelings and add to the mental health boost she gets from raving. “I feel like my brain’s reconnecting in ways that it has forgotten how to connect,” she says. “I can get down with what’s going on in my life at times, and it completely transforms me into a much more positive person.”

Wellness advice in your 40s, 50s, and beyond is often the same advice over and over: protect your sleep, drink less, manage stress, and stick to a routine. But in contrast, this group of ravers finds genuine self-care in the act of staying out late, dancing for hours, and disrupting those prescribed wellness rules. “In this world where everything is so optimized and planned and scheduled, there is something that we lose in terms of fun,” says Liddle, noting that raving brings it to the forefront. The key is to accept the occasional trade-off—less sleep in the name of mental health benefits—and to strike a balance between partying and recovering.

Manson has attended a couple of Daybreaker events, which are morning, sober parties and raves, often starting around 6 a.m. Early parties like these are becoming more common. O’Grady adds that more women DJs are putting on earlier shows with the attitude of: “We all want to get together, we all want to have a dance, but we want to be in bed by midnight.”

However, Manson prefers later shows because she finds that’s when more traditional EDM is played. But staying up until 4 a.m. at these events has been a bit of a learning curve, so she tries to limit her events to one per weekend. “The enthusiasm's there, but I'm not prepared to spend so much time recovering,” she says. “Once is great, it does what I want it to do. It makes me feel good. I get to connect with people that I enjoy spending time with.” She prioritizes sleeping in the next morning, and just rests the next day if she needs to. Then, she can still go to the gym and take long walks during the week. (She doesn’t work anymore, so she has more flexibility to rest.)

Despite the missed-out-on sleep, Karen D. finds that rave life rejuvenates her. “If I've been away at a festival for a weekend, I come back very tired because I need more sleep,” she says. “However, I do feel refreshed somehow—more clearheaded.”

But she still makes sure to still get seven hours of sleep if she goes to bed late, so then she can still fulfill her responsibilities at home, like taking her grandson to school. The tradeoff is also worth it for her, and in fact, going to raves inadvertently benefits her wellness routine. It “really helps motivate me to do weight training, to go running, to do all these wholesome recognized exercises, because I want to stay well to be able to go and dance [until] 3 o'clock in the morning,” she says.

Rave culture is no longer just for younger people, and women in midlife are soaking in every ounce of fun, freedom, community, and release. “They don't want to be defined by their age, but more importantly, they don't want to be restricted by it,” says O’Grady. “Saying, ‘I want to dress up in my sequins, I want to put my face on, I want to go and have a dance, I want to stay out all night and shrug off my responsibilities for a little while, I want all of that and why shouldn't I?’”

For Manson, getting ready is part of the appeal, and she’s collected a variety of vibrant, fun outfits to go out in. “It's almost like creating a bit of an identity, which I'm quite enjoying,” she says. At this stage of life, raving has given her a way to reinvent herself.

Midlife can chip away at a woman’s confidence and leave her feeling overlooked. Raving pushes back on that by giving women a place to be bold and seen. As Karen D. puts it, “Women of my age can often disappear or become invisible, and it's almost the opposite of that.”

Since her husband’s death, Manson has made a point of pushing herself to try new things. Raving has given her lasting memories, a fresh outlook, and a crew of friends who aren’t ready to stop dancing anytime soon. “I live with the feeling that life’s very short and precious,” she says, “so seize the moment.”
